toc.title: What sleep needs, through the Polyvagal Theory
Why stress is a big deal

blocks.p: Are you tossing and turning at night, plagued by worries and anxieties? You're not alone. Stress-induced insomnia is a common sleep disorder that affects many people. But what's the connection between stress and insomnia? I want to look at this relationship through the lens of neurophysiology, because I want you to be able to sleep better. I want you well rested and more able to self-regulate, and I suspect you want the same thing.

Stress is a natural response to threats or challenges, even minor things you might not be aware of. You could feel stress in response to major life changes, like moving, or a new boss coming into your workplace. But there are also smaller things that induce stress that we don't normally consider: crowds, or constant background noise. Even a low hum in the background might induce stress, and these things are not so obvious.

What's happening is that these sounds and contexts trigger the body's sympathetic mobilization system, which is responsible for flight and fight when we're in danger. In other words, when we're stressed, we're prepared for survival in a sense. We're ready to either confront danger or escape it.

But these day-to-day things aren't things we can exactly run away from or fight off. You can't fight the background hum of traffic. You can't really run away from the refrigerator hum, or the AC banging on and then humming in the background constantly. Yes, you could turn the AC off, but then you might be super hot, and you can't really run away from or fight that off either.
These small things we might not even be aware of accumulate in the body, and we feel them as stress, as chronic stress. That can lead to many problems, including insomnia.

Stress impacts the sleep cycle. It makes it difficult to fall asleep or stay asleep. And that can lead to a vicious cycle: stress leads to poor sleep, which leads to more stress during the day, which leads to poor sleep. It's self-reinforcing, and it can impact your overall well-being.

Even when you do sleep, you may have non-restorative sleep. It isn't refreshing, and that leads to more stress, or feeling tired and groggy the next day. Mild to moderate dysregulation, maybe severe dysregulation.

That cycle might set you up the next day for negative coping mechanisms: alcohol, drug use, maybe sleeping through work. You might be more irritated and snappy with your family. Those negative coping mechanisms and impulsive behaviors you'll regret later add to the stress, and now you also feel regret and shame, blame, and self-judgment. The issue compounds on itself. And to deal with that compounding, you're likely to return to those negative coping habits. Again, a self-reinforcing cycle.

blocks.h: What sleep needs, through the Polyvagal Theory

blocks.p: What's necessary for sleep, to stop this process? We can frame it in terms of the Polyvagal Theory.

The Polyvagal Theory is basically the science of connection and how we respond to danger. One of its teachings is that we actually have two parasympathetic nervous systems. One of those biological pathways is responsible for safety, for social engagement while we're safe. It's called the social engagement system. The other is responsible for immobilization when our life is under threat. When the body detects that death is imminent, immobilization may be the response.

And of course we have the sympathetic system, which is responsible for flight and fight, for mobilization. When we remain in flight or fight for too long, that results in stress. The body is prepared for danger. So someone who's stressed is not exiting their mobilization state. They cannot, or are not yet, accessing the body's natural states of safety and immobilization.

To fall asleep, we need both of those parasympathetic states. We have to be immobile. You're not going to fall asleep while you're running. You have to be lying down, maybe sitting. And you have to be safe. You have to feel safe in your body. Safety and immobility active together result in a mixed state called stillness.
So to fall asleep, you have to be able to immobilize and feel safe. In stress, you're not feeling safe. The body is prepared for danger.

blocks.h: Why stress is a big deal

blocks.p: Stress impacts not just one system, like your autonomic nervous system, but multiple systems. It has a negative impact on your overall health: your mental health, and your physical health as well.

Some evidence of this is the Adverse Childhood Experiences study. This was from, I believe, the '90s. They surveyed thousands and thousands of people and found that adverse experiences in early childhood led to negative health impacts later in life: mental, behavioral, and physical. The study also found that the more adverse childhood experiences there were, the greater the number and severity of those symptoms. The idea is that those experiences added stress to the body. Sometimes they were flat-out traumatic, but here we're focusing on the stress, the constant state of flight or fight.
That constant state:

ul: can affect the cardiovascular system, leading to high blood pressure and other heart-related issues.
can impact the digestive system, exacerbating stomach aches, ulcers, and other digestive problems.
can weaken the immune system, making you more susceptible to infections.
can affect the musculoskeletal system, leading to muscle contractions and restricted blood flow.
can impact the nervous system, leading to anxiety, depression, and other mental health issues.

blocks.p: So stress is a big deal. And sleep, as part of breaking the stress and insomnia cycle, is a big deal. To break the cycle, immobilization while safe, that mixed state of stillness, is really important.

I contributed to an article for Sleepopolis as part of the Polyvagal Institute's board of editors, and it's a pretty fun one. It's about something on TikTok called vagal nerve icing. Someone claims they're stimulating their vagal nerve by putting a bag of frozen peas on their chest to help them fall asleep.

To get to sleep, you might be doing stuff like that, things you find on TikTok, and crossing your fingers and hoping for the best. If it helps, awesome. I'm super happy for you. And talk to your doctor about it, because you might have some issue that precludes frozen stuff being placed on your chest. That's between you and your doctor. I'm not recommending it. If you want to do these vagal hacks you find randomly, go ahead.
But instead of relying on frozen peas night after night, I do think there's a better, more sustainable option.

I don't want you to wait for insomnia to be a problem night after night. You have to practice ahead of time, and that means being in your polyvagal state of safety: the state of connection, whether it's with somebody else, with yourself, or with your environment through your senses.

Practice feeling safety during the day: when you're with your pets, when you're out walking, when you're cooking dinner. Mindfully use your senses. Use your body's capacity for safety. Welcome it with curiosity. As you build the strength of your safety state, exercising it like anything else, defensive activation won't be as out of control, eventually.

You'll know you're in your safety state because you'll be able to breathe in your belly. You'll be more connected to your senses, to yourself, your pets, or your spouse. You'll be able to smile. You'll be thinking more positively. Those are all signs of your safety state, so practice doing things that bring you to those experiences.

blocks.why: This article is about practicing. This is the practice built from your check-ins.

blocks.p: The other thing you can do, which I think is pretty easy for the most part, is change your environment. I don't mean move. I mean look at your environment at night and ask yourself how you feel about it.

If you don't do well in the dark, that's something you can probably change. If you do well with dark but a little bit of light, you can change that. Whether you do well with a sound machine on, or with complete silence, or sleeping under the covers: those are things you can change to make an impact pretty quickly.

What you're doing is setting up your environment to give you passive cues of safety. Passive safety cues are things you don't have to think about or do anything with. You set them up once, and then night after night they give you cues of safety that help activate your safety state and keep you in it.

So at night, see how you feel about things, and see what you can change. During the day, make some changes and practice being in your safety state. Then at night, see how it feels. Maybe it'll feel a little different. If there's a little less insomnia, a little less anxiety, a little less stress, that's probably a good thing. Then ask yourself, "What else can I do? What else can I change?" Eventually, and hopefully sooner rather than later, you'll have an environment that gives you more passive cues of safety than anything else.
If you can do that, then the active things you can do to anchor in safety, like breathing deeply, using your imagination, singing, or doing something creative, might be more beneficial.

If you're white-knuckling it every night and praying those peas will solve your problems, I don't think that's going to be as effective as practicing this stuff ahead of time and doing the best you can to set yourself up for success. If you wait for the insomnia, if you wait for the stress to get too far before you do something about it, you're setting yourself up for the same problem over and over again.
So here's what I'd ask you to do: what can you alter in your environment, and what can you do now to help access your safety state?
